beats.say: Open like a teacher: two skills today, ordering numbers (which is bigger) and rounding (a close, friendly number). Both depend on place value. No questions.

lines.say: Here are two numbers that look almost the same: four thousand eight hundred and twenty-five, and four thousand two hundred and eighty-five. Which one is bigger? There's a clever way to decide without guessing.

lines.text: Today: ORDER numbers, then ROUND them
lines.say: Today we'll learn two things. How to put numbers in order, and how to round a number to a friendlier one that's close to it. Both come from place value.

beats.say: Comparing: start at the LEFT, the biggest place. Compare thousands, then hundreds... Mark the first place that differs. Use 4825 vs 4285. No questions.

lines.say: Here's the rule. Always start at the left, with the biggest place. Compare the thousands first.
Both have four thousands, so it's a tie. Nothing to decide yet. Move on to the next place.
Now the hundreds. One has eight hundreds, the other has only two. Eight is more than two, so we have our winner.
So four thousand eight hundred and twenty-five is greater than four thousand two hundred and eighty-five. We don't even need to look at the tens and ones. The first place that is different decides.

beats.say: Order three numbers from smallest to greatest: 5031, 5310, 5103. Walk through: same thousands, compare hundreds. No questions.

lines.say: Let's put these three in order, smallest to greatest. They all start with five thousand, so I look at the hundreds.
Zero hundreds, three hundreds, one hundred. So the smallest is the one with no hundreds, which is 5031.
Then one hundred beats nothing, and three hundreds beats one hundred. In order, smallest first: 5031, then 5103, then 5310.

beats.say: A friend compares from the right end (looks at ones first). Test it on 3299 vs 3301 and show it fails. Detective tone.

lines.say: A friend of mine says: just look at the end digits. Nine is bigger than one, so 3299 is bigger than 3301. Let's test that.
Using our rule from the left: thousands tie. Then hundreds: two hundreds against three hundreds. Three hundreds wins, so 3301 is the bigger number.
My friend's idea fails because the ones are the smallest place. The biggest place that differs is what counts.

beats.say: Rounding to the nearest ten, with the number line picture: 48 is between 40 and 50, past the halfway mark 45. Look at the ones digit: 5 or more round up, less than 5 round down. Do 48 and 43. No questions.

lines.say: Rounding means finding the nearest friendly number. Look at forty-eight on the number line. It sits between forty and fifty, and the halfway mark is forty-five. Which is it closer to?
Here's the trick. Look at the ones digit. It's an 8, which is five or more, and on the line 48 is past the halfway mark, so the number climbs up to the next ten.
Forty-eight rounds up to fifty.
Now forty-three. It has a 3 in the ones place, less than five, so it stays down at forty.

lines.text: 5 or more: round UP.  Less than 5: round DOWN.
lines.say: So: five or more, round up. Less than five, round down.

beats.say: Rounding to the nearest hundred, with the number line picture: 830 sits between 800 and 900, below the halfway mark 850. Look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to: the tens digit. Do 830 -> 800 and 850 -> 900, then warn about the slip of looking at the hundreds digit. No questions.

lines.say: Now the nearest hundred. Look at eight hundred and thirty. It sits between eight hundred and nine hundred, and the halfway mark is eight hundred and fifty.

To round to the nearest hundred, we look at the tens digit, the one right next door. In 830 the tens digit is a 3, less than five, so it rounds down to eight hundred. But exactly 850 has a 5 in the tens place, so by our rule it goes up to nine hundred.

lines.text: Look at the digit one place to the RIGHT
lines.say: The rule never changes, whatever place you round to. A common slip is to look at the hundreds digit, the 8, which would wrongly send 830 all the way up to 900. Peek at the neighbour on the right-hand side, and let that digit decide.

beats.say: Do one TOGETHER: round 2586 to the nearest ten and nearest hundred. Each question is written on the board first.

lines.say: Now you help me. Two thousand five hundred and eighty-six. We'll round it two ways.

lines.text: Nearest ten: look at the ones digit, 6, so round UP → 2590
lines.say: The ones digit is 6, five or more, so we go up.

ask.prompt: Round 2586 to the nearest ten. Which digit do you look at?
ask.onMiss: Ask: which digit is in the ones place? Is it five or more?

lines.text: Nearest hundred: look at the tens digit, 8, so round UP → 2600
lines.say: Eight tens means we climb up past the next hundred.

ask.prompt: Now round 2586 to the nearest hundred.
ask.onMiss: Ask: which digit is in the tens place? What does it tell us?

beats.say: Child works alone: order 4080, 4008, 4800, 4088; round 6753 to the nearest hundred; explain which digit decides. Hints only if stuck.

lines.say: Your turn to lead. Put these four numbers in order, smallest first.

ask.prompt: Put these in order, smallest to greatest: 4080, 4008, 4800, 4088.
ask.onMiss: Ask: same thousands for all. Which hundreds digit is biggest? Then compare the tens.

lines.say: The tens digit is 5, so we round up to six thousand eight hundred.

ask.onMiss: Ask: which digit is in the tens place? Is it five or more?

lines.text: Rounding to a place: the digit to its right decides
lines.say: The digit just to the right of the place tells us whether to round up or stay.

ask.prompt: In your own words: when you round to the nearest hundred, which digit decides?
ask.lookFor: The tens digit, the one just to the right of the hundreds place.
ask.onMiss: Ask: for the nearest ten we looked at the ones. So for the nearest hundred we look at...
